Purify

PYOOR-uh-fy -- Latin purus, 'clean, unmixed,' plus -fy, 'to make': to make pure. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To purify to remove contaminants from something.

Villagers boil the river water to purify it before anyone takes a drink.

Worked Example

An engineer runs cloudy well water through layers of sand, charcoal, and fine mesh until what drips out the other end is perfectly clear and safe to drink.

Removing contaminants until something is clean is exactly what it means to purify. Unlike 'dilute,' which only weakens impurities by adding more liquid, purify actually takes the impurities out.

How Purify Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

cleanse

cleanse: to clean something thoroughly

distill

distill: to purify a liquid by heating and condensing it

filter: to remove particles by passing something through a barrier

Antonyms

contaminate

contaminate: to make something impure or unsafe

pollute

pollute: to make dirty or harmful

How Strong Is It? — cleanse → distill → purify

cleanse vs. purify

cleanse vs. purify: Cleanse is broader and often gentler than purify -- you can cleanse a surface or a wound, while purify insists that contaminants are removed until something is truly pure.

distill vs. purify

distill vs. purify: Distill is a stronger, more technical cousin of purify: to purify is to remove contaminants by any means, while to distill is to boil and re-condense a liquid until only its purest essence remains.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — pur-

root — pur-: pure, clean, unmixed (Latin (purus))

suffix — -ify

suffix — -ify: to make (Latin (facere, 'to make'))

Put it together

Put it together: Latin purus meant 'clean, unmixed,' and the -ify ending, from facere ('to make'), turns it into an action -- to purify is literally 'to make pure,' the same root behind pure and purity.
